newsitem.title: USA: AMR reports drop in profits, cites labor dispute.
newsitem.headline: AMR reports drop in profits, cites labor dispute.

text.p: American Airlines parent AMR Corp. said Wednesday a bitter labour dispute with pilots hurt its first-quarter profits and forced it to delay delivery on at least 14 Boeing jets scheduled for next year.
Fort Worth, Texas-based AMR posted quarterly net income of $152 million, or $1.65 per share, compared with $157 million, or $2.02 per share, in the same period last year.

Company executives said the pilots' contract dispute had a negative impact of $70 million on net earnings in the quarter because passengers turned away from American, the nation's No. 2 airline, in the weeks leading up to a brief February strike.
The company also had higher operating expenses compared with the year-ago quarter.
Nevertheless, AMR's earnings handily beat Wall Street expectations of $1.47 per share, and AMR stock climbed $2.375 to end the day at $85 on the New York Stock Exchange.

"Despite the effects of a threatened pilot strike, strong levels of demand, combined with relatively limited capacity additions, produced good results for us," AMR Chairman Robert Crandall said in a statement.
"While our results are testimony to the continuing strength of demand, they would have been dramatically better absent the labour dispute," Crandall said.
Operating revenues rose to $4.4 billion from $4.3 billion a year ago.
Pilots briefly shut down the carrier Feb. 15, but President Clinton quickly ordered them back to work and set up a presidential board to help negotiate a new contract.
American's negotiatiors and union leaders reached agreement on a new tentative contract last month and pilots are now expected to approve the deal, averting the prospect of a second strike.
The tentative five-year contract includes a 9 percent wage increase and 5.75 million stock options. AMR said it took a $20 million pretax charge in the first quarter for the stock options.
AMR's chief financial officer, Gerard Arpey, said the pilots' dispute also forced American to hold off on delivery of at least 14 Boeing Co. jets scheduled for 1998.
Under a deal signed with Boeing last November, American agreed to buy 103 jetliners worth more than $6 billion by the year 2001 and acquired options on 527 more.

AMR said the deal was contingent on pilots accepting a new contract. When pilots rejected an initial tentative accord in January, American held off on putting in firm jet purchase orders, so Boeing sold many of the delivery positions it had slated for American.
Arpey told reporters American could not now take delivery of 14 Boeing 737s in 1998, and that 12 Boeing 757s scheduled for 1998 and 1999 were in question.
He said Boeing and AMR officials would meet in the next few weeks to work out a rejigged timetable for delivery of the planes. "We've got a lot of work to do."

Arpey said the new pilots' contract means American will have higher costs than its competitors over the next two years but pointed out that the gap would narrow when rivals go through new rounds of contract talks with their own workers.
"We think over the long run our costs are going to be in line with the major carriers," Arpey said.

AMR's total operating expenses were $3.7 billion in the first quarter, up from $3.6 billion last year. American Airlines' fuel costs increased 16.9 percent to 74.7 cents a gallon in the first quarter and total aircraft fuel expenses were $520 million, up from $441 million last year.
